title: How to Use This Book
coreMove: Start with the smallest clear script that protects the limit: Green for first clarity, Yellow for ignored clarity, Red for follow-through after a pattern.

exampleSpecs.audience: front-desk staff who need quick boundary language
exampleSpecs.stakes: A rushed enforcement line can turn a missed sign into a needless confrontation.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The protagonist notices their own over-escalation and resets from Red toward Green.

exampleSpecs.stakes: A reply sent while the nervous system is hot can become the new problem.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: A written memo carries the scene and shows the 24-hour pause shaping the next message.

exampleSpecs.audience: members and staff sharing limited equipment
exampleSpecs.stakes: The same closing rule can land as clear help or sudden anger.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Two named people approach one limit in opposite ways and the outcomes diverge.

exampleSpecs.audience: people who fear scripts will sound fake
exampleSpecs.stakes: Rejecting prepared language can leave a stressed person with only panic or overexplaining.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: A peer reframes scripts as rehearsal rather than imitation.

exampleSpecs.audience: new trainees learning graded boundary language
exampleSpecs.stakes: A learner may confuse firmness with starting at the highest level.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The learner's confusion becomes the material for teaching the color ladder.

exampleSpecs.audience: small service teams handling repeated no-shows
exampleSpecs.stakes: A team needs firm follow-through without turning one missed pickup into a punishment.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The same process changes after a pause is added before charged messages.
